item.title: Speech Synthesis at Long Distance: A 1h 58m Novel vs. 14 Test Phrases
item.description:
In the first article of the series, there was a table showing how a synthesized voice read an entire book: Shamil Aladin's novel "Merdiven" ("The Staircase"), 16 chapters, 15,444 words, 1 hour 58 minutes of playback. In the second, I promised to explain in detail what broke down over the long haul. Here it is. In short, the voice held up steadily for the entire two hours. Almost everything that broke was not in the model itself, but in the surrounding pipeline: text segmentation into sentences, stitching short phrases, trimming breaths, extracting text from the book file, and time-stamping. The test set of 14 phrases, which I previously used to compare model versions, didn't catch any of these problems, and in one case, couldn't distinguish a good edit from a harmful one. A disclaimer, as in previous articles in the series: model names, data sources, internal scripts, and training/decoding parameters will not be mentioned here. There will be metrics, testing methodology, and pitfalls. Read on.

item.title: DIY AI Text Detector: What AI Slop Code Catches and What's Left for a Human Editor
item.description:
I've broken down 12 signs of AI slop, i.e., text generated by a neural network and not proofread, into checks for my AI text detector. Five are caught by code, two of which are partially. The remaining seven rely solely on editor rules. Two typical introductory phrases, 'In this article, we will consider' and 'The conclusion is simple:' were missed by the script. Online detectors respond with a percentage and don't specify what to fix. The percentage itself is also unreliable: in the work of Liang et al., seven detectors on average classified 61% of TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers as machine-generated. OpenAI closed its classifier in the summer of 2023 due to low accuracy. A narrow check works differently: it names the phrase and the rule, and each trigger can be disputed separately. Wikipedia editors maintain an open list of AI text indicators and explicitly state that an indicator points to a potential problem and proves nothing on its own. My script operates on the same principle: it looks for traces of unedited text, it does not determine authorship. The overall score of this detector has already been discussed on Habr. Read more

item.title: Why I No Longer Use Pull Requests
item.description:
In February of this year, I, Alex Gusev, handed over @teqfw/di to a Codex agent for rewriting — a library I had been developing since 2019 and had meticulously crafted line by line. I wrote about this on Habr at the time. Since then, I haven't written program code manually. Not because I forgot how. It's just that agents do this work now. At the same time, Pull Requests have almost disappeared from my development process. I haven't stopped using GitHub or abandoned result verification. I simply no longer need the procedure where someone prepares a code change, and I decide whether to accept it or not. I didn't arrive at this conclusion immediately. Read more

item.title: I Wrote 61 Tests for an AI Mentor. Then I Found Out Tests Can't Be Trusted Either
item.description:
You don't hire a tutor based on their resume. You give them a real student's notebook and see not whether they know the answer, but where they'll get stuck. Will they point out the line with the error, or rewrite the problem for the student? Will they say 'I don't know, let's check,' or confidently make something up? A month ago, I integrated an AI mentor into my educational platform: it sees lessons, student progress, and their latest attempt at a task. To avoid choosing a model and tweaking prompts based on gut feeling, I set up a testing environment with automated checks and started making decisions based on its metrics. A week later, I discovered the environment itself was flawed. It accepted incomplete answers, missed a complete solution submitted under a different variable name, and failed a correct refusal. Another week later, the model in the environment behaved flawlessly, but on production for the same class of questions – it didn't. This article is about how the testing environment is set up, what it helped solve, where it created false confidence, and how I ultimately stopped trusting the model altogether. Where the environment lied.

item.title: I Set Up a Project Institute for Small Models: Weak Sectioning Gave Fourfold Improvement, a Swarm Five Points
item.description:
I am a thermal engineer, head of a department in a design organization, with fourteen years in design. I've never been a programmer, and I've been tinkering with neural networks for less than a year. This spring, I set out to grow a swarm from weak local models that would be smarter than the strongest one. The swarm didn't get smarter. However, along the way, I broke down six small models according to the scheme that any design institute works by, and measured what this scheme can handle under load. Only sectioning holds up, and it benefits a weak model more than a strong one. Read more

item.title: 1C Partner. Is it worth it?
item.description:
What solves it: expensive and lengthy fine-tuning of a narrow model, or a good wrapper around a standard cloud one? At first glance, a vendor model with unlimited and privileged access to 1C materials leaves no chance for competitors. Is there a practical advantage? We assembled an interactive assistant on an open-source stack and compared it with 1C-Partner on seven questions from the daily work of users and developers. Read more
